title: Χελώνη καὶ ἀετός
part: The Tortoise and the Eagle (Chambry 351 · Perry 230)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 351 (= Perry 230). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Χελώνη ἀετοῦ ἐδεῖτο ἵπτασθαι αὐτὴν διδάξαι.
sentences.tr: Chelōnē aetou edeito hiptasthai autēn didaxai.
sentences.l: A tortoise kept begging an eagle to teach her to fly.
sentences.n: δέομαι, 'ask, beg', takes the genitive of the person asked, ἀετοῦ, and an infinitive for the thing wanted. αὐτήν is at once the object of διδάξαι and the subject of ἵπτασθαι. The imperfect ἐδεῖτο already suggests asking that goes on and on, which the next line takes up.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ παραινοῦντος πόρρω τοῦτο τῆς φύσεως αὐτῆς εἶναι, ἐκείνη μᾶλλον τῇ δεήσει προσέκειτο.
sentences.tr: Tou de parainountos porrō touto tēs physeōs autēs einai, ekeinē mallon tēi deēsei prosekeito.
sentences.l: And he advising that this was far from her nature, she pressed the more with her entreaty.
sentences.i: When he warned her that this lay far from her nature, she only pressed her request the harder.
sentences.n: Another genitive absolute (Τοῦ δὲ παραινοῦντος), with an accusative-and-infinitive hanging from it. πόρρω takes the genitive of what a thing is far from. πρόσκειμαι with the dative is to lie hard against a thing, and so to keep pressing it.

sentences.t: Λαβὼν οὖν αὐτὴν τοῖς ὄνυξι καὶ εἰς ὕψος ἀνενεγκών, εἶτ’ ἀφῆκεν.
sentences.tr: Labōn oun autēn tois onyxi kai eis hypsos anenenkōn, eit’ aphēken.
sentences.l: So having taken her in his talons and having carried her up on high, he then let her go.
sentences.i: So he took her up in his talons, carried her high into the air, and then let her go.
sentences.n: The aorist-participle chain does the work again: two participles carry the action and the finite verb ἀφῆκεν ends it. εἶτ’, 'then', picks the sentence up after the participles — a Greek habit that English keeps with 'and then'.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ κατὰ πετρῶν πεσοῦσα συνετρίβη.
sentences.tr: Hē de kata petrōn pesousa synetribē.
sentences.l: And she, having fallen down upon rocks, was shattered.
sentences.i: She fell down upon the rocks and was broken to pieces.
sentences.n: κατά with the genitive is 'down upon, down over'. συνετρίβη is the aorist passive of συντρίβω, to grind together and so to break in pieces.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι πολλοὶ ἐν φιλονεικίαις τῶν φρονιμωτέρων παρακούσαντες ἑαυτοὺς ἔβλαψαν.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti polloi en philoneikiais tōn phronimōterōn parakousantes heautous eblapsan.
sentences.l: The fable shows that many, in contentions, having paid no heed to those wiser than themselves, harmed themselves.
sentences.i: The fable shows that many men, in their contentiousness, pay no heed to those with more sense than themselves, and do themselves harm.
sentences.n: παρακούω is to hear beside the point — to hear and not heed — and takes the genitive of the person disregarded. φρονιμωτέρων is a comparative without an expressed 'than', 'those with more sense than they'. ἔβλαψαν is a gnomic aorist, a standing truth put in past time, which is the regular idiom of these morals.
